narrative:
The model estimated a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was denied because the admissions decision relied on that risk estimate. This does not mean success is impossible; it means that, based on students with similar records, your profile was placed on the higher-risk side.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank. You were in the 3rd decile, compared with an average around the 6th decile among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The second factor was your family income bracket, which the model treated as adding to the failure risk when combined with your academic indicators. The third was your undergraduate GPA: at 2.90 versus an average of 3.23 among accepted students, it also pushed toward failure rather than passing. Your first-year rank and LSAT score were part of your broader profile, but they were not among the three most influential factors in this decision.

To improve a future application, focus on what you can still change: retake the LSAT if a higher score is realistic, take additional rigorous coursework to show academic readiness, gain law-related work or volunteer experience, and ask admissions counselors to help you address the weak points in your record. Consider applying after you have stronger evidence of academic preparation.
